summary: Describes the architecture for SPIRITS services, which start in the telephone network and need to interact with the Internet. It explains how the two worlds are connected.

plainLanguage.summary: It shows how a phone call can ask the Internet for help, like a doorbell that also rings a computer.

questions: how to forward calls from internet
subtitle: How phone calls can ask the Internet to do things on the caller's behalf

tldr.problem: Phone networks (PSTN) and the Internet operate separately. When a call arrives, there is no standard way to notify Internet-connected devices or let the caller control what happens to the call from the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: SPIRITS (Service in the PSTN Requesting Internet Services) defines an architecture with interconnected components: the PSTN detects an incoming call, a SPIRITS Client in the phone network contacts a SPIRITS Server on the user's PC over the Internet, and the user can then respond from their computer.
tldr.outcome: Services like Internet Call Waiting (notifying a user of an incoming call while online), Caller-ID Delivery (showing who is calling on the user's screen), and Call Forwarding (routing calls from the Internet) become possible.

facts.label: User activation
facts.value: Service session registration with optional lifespan

today: RFC 3136 is an Informational RFC from June 2001. It describes the SPIRITS architecture for connecting phone networks and the Internet. Later RFCs defined the SPIRITS protocol specification in more detail.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SPIRITS stands for Service in the PSTN Requesting Internet Services. This RFC describes an architecture for services that originate in the phone network (PSTN, the Public Switched Telephone Network) but need to interact with the Internet. Common examples are Internet Call Waiting, Caller-ID Delivery, and Call Forwarding.

The architecture defines the components that make up the system and the interfaces (connection points) between them. The key insight is that when an incoming phone call is detected, the phone network can send a message to an Internet-connected device asking what to do, and the device can respond by telling the phone network how to handle the call.
sections.plainLanguage: SPIRITS is a way to let the phone network talk to computers on the Internet. When a call comes in, the phone network can ask your computer: "There is a call. What should I do?"

sections.title: The Three Example Services
sections.content:
Internet Call Waiting (ICW) lets a user engaged in an Internet dial-up session know when a call arrives on the same phone line. The user can then accept the call (disconnecting the Internet), forward it to another number, redirect it to voicemail, or play a recorded message and disconnect. The user specifies how to treat the call either on the fly or with pre-set rules.

Internet Caller-ID Delivery displays the caller's number or name on the user's screen while the user is connected to the Internet. Internet Call Forwarding allows the user to forward an incoming call to another number from the Internet without interrupting their online session.
sections.plainLanguage: ICW tells you someone is calling. Caller-ID shows you who is calling. Call Forwarding lets you send the call somewhere else, all from your computer.

sections.title: SPIRITS Architecture and Components
sections.content:
The architecture includes seven main entities. In the PSTN side: the Service Control Function (SCF) executes service logic (deciding what to do with a call); the Service Switching Function (SSF) resides in switches and recognizes triggers for services; and a SPIRITS Client receives requests from the SCF and sends responses back.

On the Internet side: a PINT Server receives requests from the PINT Client (on the user's PC) and relays them to the PSTN. A SPIRITS Gateway acts as an intermediary between the SPIRITS Server and SPIRITS Client. Finally, the SPIRITS Server (on the user's PC) terminates PSTN requests and handles all interactions with the user.

The interfaces are labeled A through E: A carries PINT requests to the PINT Server; B carries notifications and user responses between the subscriber's PC and the SPIRITS Gateway; C carries communications between SPIRITS Client and Gateway; D carries parameters from the SCF to the SPIRITS Client and user disposition back; and E carries PINT requests from the PINT Server to the SCF for execution.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone network has a control center (SCF) and switches (SSF). Your computer has a server (SPIRITS Server) and a client program (PINT Client). Messages flow between them over named connections (A, B, C, D, E).

sections.title: How a Service Session Works
sections.content:
A user first subscribes to a SPIRITS service (either by phone, mail, or the web) and loads software on their PC with their PIN and the IP addresses of the SPIRITS servers. The user then activates the service by registering a service session, which can specify the session's lifespan. While the session is active, SPIRITS services are enabled.

When a call arrives during an active session, the SSF detects the call trigger, the SCF executes service logic, and the SPIRITS Client contacts the SPIRITS Gateway with the incoming call details. The SPIRITS Server on the user's PC is notified via the B interface (over the public Internet). The user can respond immediately with a call treatment (accept, forward, voicemail, reject, etc.), and the SCF transforms that response into actions like playing an announcement or resuming call processing in the switch.
sections.plainLanguage: You turn on the service. A call comes in. Your computer gets a message asking what to do. You reply. The phone network does what you asked.

sections.title: Security Concerns and Protections
sections.content:
The B interface (between the subscriber's PC and SPIRITS Gateway) travels across the public Internet and is most vulnerable to theft and denial-of-service attacks. The C interface (between SPIRITS Client and SPIRITS Gateway) is typically on a service provider's intranet, where security is controlled by the provider.

Since at least one host (the PINT Gateway) is connected to the Internet, special measures like firewalls are needed to protect the C interface and the rest of the network. Detailed security requirements are found in RFC 2848, which covers the PINT Service Protocol. Because the PINT Client and SPIRITS Server are co-located on the user's PC, security requirements for the A and B interfaces are identical.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages sent over the Internet (interface B) can be stolen or interrupted, so they need encryption and protection. The phone network side is usually safer.
